options.rationale: Explaining costs nothing and changes how it is experienced.

options.text: Refer the whole matter to your supervisor and take no action
options.rationale: Deferring is itself a decision, and it usually leaves the patient waiting.

items.explanation_md: Most of the room for ethical judgment at this level is in how an obligation is carried out, not whether it is. That room is real and it matters to people.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

items.stem: Which of these is settled by your state rather than by anything in this module?

options.text: The age at which a minor may consent, and what must be reported to whom
options.rationale: Both are state law, and both vary considerably.

options.text: The four elements of negligence
options.rationale: The elements are common to the doctrine.

options.text: The four abilities that make up capacity
options.rationale: That framework does not change at a state line.

options.text: Whether a blank section on a portable order means full treatment
options.rationale: That default is a feature of the form standard.

items.explanation_md: Knowing which parts of this chapter are portable and which are local is itself part of the content. Everything local belongs in the overlay, not in memory.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

stimulus.text:
2210. An 81-year-old man at home, called by his daughter for "not acting right". He is pale and clammy, with a blood glucose of 39 mg/dL. He is drowsy and will not answer questions.

On the refrigerator is a portable medical order form in his name. Section A — cardiopulmonary resuscitation — is completely unmarked. Section B is ticked for selective treatment. The clinician has signed it.

You give glucose. Ten minutes later he is alert, oriented, arguing, and says he is not going anywhere. His daughter tells you to take him whether he likes it or not, and that the form on the fridge means he does not want treatment.

items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

items.stem: On arrival he is drowsy and will not answer. On what basis do you treat the hypoglycemia?

options.text: Implied consent — he cannot consent and the care is needed now
options.rationale: A reasonable person would consent to treatment for symptomatic hypoglycemia.

options.text: His daughter’s consent
options.rationale: An adult daughter does not automatically have authority to consent for her father.

options.text: The portable medical order form
options.rationale: The form limits certain treatments; it does not consent to this one.

options.text: You may not treat until he is alert enough to agree
options.rationale: That reading would require the hypoglycemia to be left untreated.

items.explanation_md: Implied consent covers the emergency in front of you and nothing beyond it.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

items.stem: The daughter says the form means he does not want treatment. Is she right?

options.text: No — Section B permits selective treatment, and an unmarked Section A defaults to full resuscitation
options.rationale: The form limits nothing that is relevant to giving him glucose.

options.text: Yes — any portable medical order means comfort measures only
options.rationale: That is a serious and common misreading.

options.text: Yes, because Section A is blank
options.rationale: A blank is never read as a limitation.

options.text: It cannot be determined without contacting the signing clinician
options.rationale: The form is readable as it stands, and he is not in arrest.

items.explanation_md: Read what the form actually says. It was not written to stop anyone treating a hypoglycemic man at home, and it does not.
items.source_ref: National POLST — portable medical orders: form structure and completion standards.

items.stem: He is now alert and refusing. What has changed legally?

options.text: He may now have capacity, so implied consent no longer applies and his own decision governs
options.rationale: Capacity is assessed now, not from how he was fifteen minutes ago.

options.text: Nothing — he was incapacitated on arrival, so you may still transport him
options.rationale: Capacity is time-specific and it has plausibly returned.

options.text: His daughter now decides, as she called the ambulance
options.rationale: Calling an ambulance confers no authority over another adult.

options.text: The form now governs the decision
options.rationale: The form is about resuscitation preferences, not about this refusal.

items.explanation_md: The same patient, half an hour apart, under two different legal frameworks. That is what "decision-specific and time-specific" means in practice.
items.source_ref: Appelbaum PS. Assessment of patients’ competence to consent to treatment. N Engl J Med 2007;357:1834–40.

items.stem: Which four abilities do you assess before accepting his refusal?

options.text: That he understands what you have told him
options.rationale: Can he take in the information?

options.text: That he appreciates it applies to him
options.rationale: Not to hypoglycemic patients generally — to him, tonight.

options.text: That he can reason about the options
options.rationale: Some weighing, whether or not it matches yours.

options.text: That he can express a choice
options.rationale: Communicated, and reasonably stable.

options.text: That he agrees with your recommendation
options.rationale: The trap. He is allowed to decide against you.

items.explanation_md: Four abilities, assessed in a couple of minutes, and written down as what he said rather than as a conclusion.
items.source_ref: Appelbaum PS. Assessment of patients’ competence to consent to treatment. N Engl J Med 2007;357:1834–40.

items.stem: He has capacity and refuses. His daughter insists you take him anyway. What do you do?

options.text: Decline to transport him against his will, and say to them both why
options.rationale: Transporting a capable adult who refuses is not something a relative can authorize.

options.text: Transport him, since the daughter is next of kin
options.rationale: Next of kin does not override a capable adult.

options.text: Transport him because hypoglycemia may recur
options.rationale: A real risk, and it does not remove his right to decide.

options.text: Ask the daughter to sign a consent form on his behalf
options.rationale: She cannot consent for a capable adult, and a form does not change that.

items.explanation_md: Being right about the medicine does not give you authority over an adult who has capacity. It gives you an obligation to explain it well.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

items.stem: What belongs in the record of this refusal?

options.text: The capacity assessment as a conversation — what you asked, what he said
options.rationale: Not "alert and oriented ×4" standing in for an assessment.

options.text: The specific risk of recurrent hypoglycemia, and that you named it
options.rationale: Including what could happen if nobody is there.

options.text: That he repeated the risks back in his own words
options.rationale: The strongest single line available to you.

options.text: The plan agreed — that he eats, and that someone stays with him
options.rationale: What makes the refusal safer rather than merely documented.

options.text: That his daughter disagreed and you sided with the patient
options.rationale: Record the disagreement factually; the editorial is not useful.

items.explanation_md: A refusal note that describes a conversation and a plan is defensible. One that records a signature is not.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

items.stem: What is the single most useful thing you can say to him before leaving?

options.text: That he can call again at any time, for any reason, and nobody will hold it against him
options.rationale: It keeps the door open for the call you actually want him to make.

options.text: That he is making a serious mistake
options.rationale: He has heard it, and repeating it does not help now.

options.text: That his daughter will be responsible for him
options.rationale: Not something you can assign to her.

options.text: That you will return in an hour to check
options.rationale: Do not promise something the system will not deliver.

items.explanation_md: You want the second call to happen early. Everything in the last sixty seconds should make that easier rather than harder.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.

items.stem: Reviewing this call, which three decisions would you have to defend, and on what?

options.text: Treating on implied consent, reading the form correctly, and accepting a refusal from a patient whose capacity you assessed and recorded
options.rationale: Three distinct frameworks, each with its own evidence in the chart.

options.text: Only the decision not to transport
options.rationale: The other two would be examined just as closely.

options.text: Only the reading of the form
options.rationale: It is one of three.

options.text: None — the patient refused, so the call ends there
options.rationale: A refusal is the beginning of the scrutiny, not the end of it.

items.explanation_md: One call, three frameworks, and the record is the only thing that will still exist when someone asks. That is the whole chapter in one living room.
items.source_ref: NHTSA National EMS Education Standards (2021) — Preparatory: Medical/Legal and Ethical Issues.
